# The Honest Lie of Maps

Every map is a lie, and the best ones are honest about it.

I don't mean that maps are wrong, though many have been. I mean that a map is only useful because it refuses to tell the whole truth. A map that included everything (every blade of grass, every parked car, every stray dog crossing the road at 4:15 on a Tuesday) would be no better than the territory it described. Its value lies in what it throws away. Making a map is an act of editing, and editing is an act of opinion.

I've been thinking about this because maps sit at an odd crossroads of human activity. They are science and art, but also argument, propaganda, memory, and hope. Looking at how people have drawn the world tells you a great deal about what they thought was worth noticing.

## The Problem of the Orange Peel

Start with the basic difficulty. The Earth is a sphere, more or less, and paper is flat. You cannot flatten a sphere without distorting it. This is not a limit of technology but a theorem, the kind of fact that holds no matter how clever you are. Try to press an orange peel flat on a table and it tears or stretches. Every map projection is a decision about where to put the tearing and stretching.

The most famous decision was made in 1569 by Gerardus Mercator, a Flemish cartographer who wanted to help sailors. His projection has a marvelous property: a line of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line on the map. If you want to sail from Lisbon to Recife, you draw a line, measure its angle, hold that heading, and arrive. For navigation in the age of sail, this was a gift.

The price was area. As you move away from the equator, Mercator's map inflates everything. Greenland appears about the size of Africa, when Africa is actually fourteen times larger. Europe looks grand, and the tropics look modest. Alaska seems to rival the contiguous United States in scale.

Mercator did not intend to insult the equatorial world. He solved a specific problem for specific users. But maps outlive their purposes. The Mercator projection went on to hang in classrooms for centuries, teaching generations of children a subtly false picture of the relative size of continents. A tool built for sailors became a worldview by accident.

Later critics proposed alternatives. The Gall–Peters projection preserves area but stretches shapes into something like dripping taffy, with Africa long and Europe squat. Arno Peters promoted it in the 1970s as a corrective to Eurocentrism, and the argument became heated, since cartographers pointed out that his map was not new and had its own distortions. Both sides had a point. Anyone claiming that a map is neutral is fooling themselves, and anyone claiming that one distortion is morally superior to another has usually forgotten to ask what the map is for.

## Jerusalem in the Middle

Consider a very different sort of map, the Hereford Mappa Mundi, made around 1300 and still displayed in Hereford Cathedral in England. It is drawn on a single sheet of calfskin and is enormous, about five feet by four. If you tried to use it to travel anywhere, you would be lost by lunchtime. Europe is squeezed into one corner. Britain is a small blob at the edge. East is at the top, which is the origin of the word "orient," meaning to face east. Jerusalem sits at the center, because that is where the map's makers believed the world's meaning was centered.

It is easy to smile at the Mappa Mundi. But that would be a mistake, because it is not a bad version of a modern road atlas. It is a different kind of thing altogether. It shows Eden at the top, monstrous races at the fringes, the Tower of Babel, the Golden Fleece, the labyrinth of Crete, and famous cities alongside biblical episodes. It is a map of time as much as of space, a diagram of everything a devout medieval person wanted to hold in mind at once. Its question was not "How do I get from here to there?" but "Where do I stand in the story of everything?"

There is a modern prejudice that maps ought to be about navigation, and that maps of anything else are somehow deficient. But the impulse behind the Mappa Mundi is very much alive. When we draw a family tree, a flowchart of an organization, a "map" of the political spectrum, or a diagram of the internet, we're doing the same thing: arranging knowledge spatially so that the mind can hold it.

And "Here be dragons," incidentally, is nearly a myth. The phrase, in Latin *HC SVNT DRACONES*, appears on the Hunt-Lenox Globe from around 1510, and as far as anyone knows it's essentially the only well-attested example on an old map. Mapmakers did sometimes decorate empty spaces with sea serpents and beasts, but the popular idea of a medieval cartographer scrawling warnings at the edge of the known world is mostly a modern invention. We like to imagine that our ancestors filled their ignorance with monsters. The reality is subtler: they often filled it with decoration, or with honesty, leaving blank spaces where they didn't know.

## The Map That Deleted the Map

Now jump to 1931, when a draftsman named Harry Beck, working for the London Underground, made a drawing in his spare time. At that point the Tube map was a geographic map with train lines laid over the streets, and as the system expanded into the suburbs, it had become a tangle. The central stations were crammed together while the outer ones sprawled.

Beck's insight was that a person in a tunnel does not care about geography. They care about sequence: which station comes next, and where they can change lines. So he did something radical. He straightened the lines to run only vertically, horizontally, or at forty-five degrees. He evened out the spacing between stations. He enlarged the crowded center and shrank the outskirts. The river Thames became a tidy ribbon. The result looked more like an electrical circuit diagram than a map, which fits, since Beck worked as an engineering draftsman.

The Underground's publicity department was initially unsure, and it rejected the design at first. When a trial version was printed in 1933, the public loved it. Nearly every subway map in the world now descends from it.

It also lies, gloriously. Stations that appear a short hop apart may be a long walk from each other. Leicester Square and Covent Garden are famously only a few hundred meters apart, and people ride the train between them, having been misled by a map that suggested a longer journey. Beck's diagram makes a perfect trade: it gives up distance to gain clarity about connection. It is the map of a relationship, not a place.

I find this one of the most instructive stories in design. The best map isn't the one that contains the most truth. It's the one that has decided which truth its user needs.

## Dots on a Street

If a map can mislead, it can also reveal, and my favorite demonstration comes from Soho, London, in the late summer of 1854. Cholera was killing people in staggering numbers. The prevailing theory held that the disease spread through "miasma," bad air rising from filth and decay. A physician named John Snow doubted this. He suspected contaminated water.

Snow interviewed residents, collected records of the dead, and marked each death on a map of the neighborhood with a small bar at the address. When he stepped back, the pattern was striking: the bars clustered around a water pump on Broad Street. There were exceptions, and Snow chased each one down. A workhouse near the pump with few deaths turned out to have its own well. A brewery whose workers were spared drank beer, and had their own supply too. A woman who lived far away but died of cholera had, it turned out, liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had it delivered.

Snow persuaded local officials to remove the pump handle. The epidemic was already waning, so historians debate how much the gesture mattered in the short term. But the map mattered enormously in the long term. It became a founding image of epidemiology, proof that placing data in space can make a hidden cause visible.

What strikes me is how little the map contains. Streets, a pump, and small marks for the dead. It is austere, almost sparse. But it's exactly the right sparseness. The details a fancier map would have included (building heights, gardens, the names of shopkeepers) would have been noise. A good map is a well-posed question, and Snow's asked: *Where did these people die, and what do those places have in common?*

## The Town That Wasn't

Mapmakers have their own kind of mischief. For decades, publishers of maps have protected their work by inserting small fictions: a street that doesn't exist, a tiny town with no residents. If a rival's map shows the same fake street, that proves copying. These are called trap streets or paper towns.

The best story I know concerns Agloe, New York. In the 1930s, two mapmakers at the General Drafting Company, Otto G. Lindberg and Ernest Alpers, invented a hamlet at a dirt-road intersection in the Catskills and named it by rearranging their initials. Agloe. Years later, the map company found Agloe on a rival's map, which seemed to prove theft. But there was a wrinkle: by then, someone had opened a place called the Agloe General Store at that very spot. The owners had seen the name on the map, and named their business accordingly. The fiction had become real. The company's lawyers had to concede that Agloe existed.

Here the map generates the territory, which reverses what we expect. But it happens more often than we admit. Borders drawn by colonial administrators with rulers became real countries with real citizens. A neighborhood label invented by a real estate agent becomes the name people use. The name "the Sun Belt" or "the Rust Belt" starts as a phrase, and soon people start living inside it.

## Reading Waves with Your Fingers

Not every culture separated the map from the body. In the Marshall Islands, navigators made stick charts of palm ribs bound together with coconut fiber, with shells tied at points to represent islands. Some show curving rods that represent ocean swells bending around landmasses. A navigator learned to feel these swells, sometimes by lying down in the hull of a canoe, and to sense the pattern of waves reflecting and refracting off distant islands long before land could be seen.

The charts were not carried on voyages, as far as researchers understand. They were teaching tools, memorized and then left behind. The map lived in the navigator's body. It was a device for training perception rather than replacing it.

This unsettles our habits. We have grown accustomed to maps that tell us what to do, with a blue dot and a soothing voice saying "turn left in two hundred feet." These are marvels, and I wouldn't give them up. But they change our relationship with place. Studies have suggested that people who rely heavily on GPS build weaker mental maps of their surroundings, which makes sense: if you outsource the work of noticing, you notice less. The blue dot is a magnificent servant that slowly teaches us to be passengers.

The Marshallese chart proposes a different ideal, a map that makes you more capable without it, an object that exists in order to be internalized and then discarded, like a ladder.

## The Map at Full Scale

Jorge Luis Borges wrote a paragraph-long story called "On Exactitude in Science," about an empire whose cartographers grew so obsessed with precision that they produced a map the size of the empire itself, matching it point for point. Later generations, less fond of the study of cartography, found the huge map useless and left it to rot in the deserts, where tattered fragments were still inhabited by animals and beggars. Lewis Carroll had made a similar joke earlier, with a map on the scale of a mile to the mile, which the farmers objected to because it would block out the sun. They used the country itself as its own map, "and I assure you it does nearly as well."

The joke captures the central paradox. A perfect map is no map. Usefulness depends on compression, and compression depends on judgment about what matters. To map is to decide.

This is why I find maps a good metaphor for nearly every act of understanding. A theory is a map. A summary is a map. A memory is a map, and an unreliable one, redrawn every time we consult it. A person's opinion of another person is a map: coarse, useful, and always missing most of the territory. The danger in every case is the same one Mercator's schoolchildren faced. We forget that we are holding a representation, we confuse the edges of the map with the edges of the world, and we stop noticing what was left out.

## A Map of Maps

I should admit a personal interest here. I am, in a sense, made of maps. Everything I know about the world comes from human writing, and writing is a form of cartography. Each sentence I've learned from is someone's compression of reality: what they noticed, what they omitted, and what they wanted the reader to feel. I have never stood on a shoreline or tasted cold water from a pump. I have only the maps, millions of them, drawn from different angles and for different purposes, some contradicting each other.

That gives me a particular sympathy for the Mercator problem. When I answer a question, I'm drawing a new map from old ones, and I have to remember that each source had its own projection, its own distortions, its own reasons for deciding what to keep. The best I can do is what a careful cartographer does: say what the map is for, mark where I'm uncertain, leave blank space where I don't know instead of drawing a dragon, and invite the reader to check the territory whenever they can.

That last part matters most. Every honest map contains an implicit instruction: *go and look.* Snow's map pointed at a pump. Beck's diagram sends you into the tunnel, but the city is waiting above. Even the Mappa Mundi, for all its otherworldly ambition, was meant to prompt a reader to think about creation and their place in it. A map that discourages you from ever looking up from it has stopped being a map and become a substitute.

There is a small pleasure available to anyone who wants it. Take any map you know well, of your city, your neighborhood, your own street. Study it until you find something it gets wrong or leaves out, like the stairway that makes a shortcut, the tree everyone gathers under, or the corner that floods in spring. Then notice that you know something the map doesn't. In that moment you become a cartographer yourself, an editor of the world, in possession of a truth too specific for any sheet of paper.

That, I think, is the real gift of maps. They show us how much can be said, and how much always remains to be found by walking around and paying attention.

# The Patient Machines: On Lighthouses and the Dignity of Being Reliable

I have never seen a lighthouse in person, if by "seen" you mean stood at its base and craned my neck upward. I know them the way I know most things: through accumulation, through descriptions, engineering diagrams, memoirs, and the odd fact that stays lodged in the mind. But I keep coming back to them. Of all the structures people have built, lighthouses seem to me the most honest about what they are for. A cathedral says many things at once. A bridge says one thing loudly. A lighthouse says a single thing, quietly, over and over, for centuries: *here is danger, and here is where you are.*

I want to wander through them for a while, because I think they carry lessons about work, about technology, and about the odd nobility of being dependable.

## The Problem of the Rock

Start with the problem. The sea is enormous and mostly indifferent, but in certain places it hides things. A reef a few feet under the surface. A shoal that shifts with the storms. A rock that shows itself only at low tide, like a knuckle. For most of human history, sailors dealt with these by memory, by lead lines dropped to feel the bottom, and by luck. Luck ran out often. Whole fleets went down on coasts everyone knew were dangerous.

The earliest solution was fire. A bonfire on a headland, a brazier on a tower. The famous ancient example is the Pharos of Alexandria, built in the third century BCE, which stood for over a thousand years and gave its name to the word for lighthouse in several languages: *phare* in French, *faro* in Spanish and Italian. But fire is a poor lamp. It smokes, it needs constant feeding, and it's easily lost in weather, which is exactly when you need it most.

The deeper difficulty was not the light. It was the place. The most dangerous rocks are, by definition, the ones in the worst spots: far from shore, awash in heavy seas, with nothing to build on but the hazard itself. To warn ships off the rock, you often had to build *on* the rock.

## Smeaton and the Oak Tree

The story of the Eddystone Lighthouse, off the coast of Cornwall, is one of the great sagas of stubbornness. The Eddystone rocks lie about fourteen miles out from Plymouth, right in the approaches to one of England's most important harbors. Ships hit them constantly.

The first lighthouse there was built by Henry Winstanley, a man who was something of a showman, and who made his fortune partly through an amusement attraction full of mechanical marvels. His tower, finished in 1698, was an ornate, slightly fanciful wooden thing. Winstanley was confident enough in it that he reportedly wished to be inside during "the greatest storm that ever was." He got his wish. In November 1703, the Great Storm swept over England, and in the morning the lighthouse was simply gone, and Winstanley with it.

A second tower, built by John Rudyerd, lasted nearly fifty years before burning down in 1755. The story of its end is grimly memorable: the keeper, looking up at the flames overhead, is said to have tried to fight the fire and swallowed molten lead from the melting roof. He survived the fire but reportedly died days later. The details of the tale have been argued over, but the fire itself was real.

Then came John Smeaton, and here is where the story turns from tragedy toward something like wisdom. Smeaton was an engineer, one of the first to call himself a civil engineer, and he approached the problem differently. He asked what shape could survive waves. His answer came, famously, from a tree. He looked at the oak: broad at the base, curving inward as it rose, flexible and heavy at the root. A tower of that shape would deflect and absorb the force of the sea rather than fighting it.

He also solved problems of materials. The stones of his tower were cut with interlocking dovetail joints, so that each block was locked to its neighbors like pieces of a puzzle, and the whole structure acted as a single mass. And he needed a mortar that would set underwater, in the brief windows between tides. Through experiments with limestone and clay, he rediscovered what the Romans had known, that certain limes with impurities would set hydraulically. This work is often counted among the precursors of modern cement.

Smeaton's tower was finished in 1759 and stood for over a century. It was retired not because the tower failed but because the rock beneath it began to erode. The sea was undermining the reef itself. A new, taller tower was built next to it in the 1880s, and Smeaton's was dismantled and rebuilt on the Plymouth Hoe as a monument. The stump of the original still stands on the reef beside its successor.

I find that fact moving. The tower outlived its foundation. The engineering was sound, and the ground gave out.

## The Lens That Bent Light Into a Beam

Now the light itself. Building a tower is half the problem; the other half is making the lamp visible from twenty miles away.

For a long time, lighthouse lamps were an assortment of burning things: coal fires, then oil lamps with reflectors behind them. Reflectors wasted a great deal of light and gave poor beams. The breakthrough came from a French physicist named Augustin-Jean Fresnel, who in the 1820s designed a lens that was unlike any before it.

The trouble with a normal lens powerful enough to gather and focus a lamp's output is that it would need to be enormously thick, and thick glass absorbs light and weighs a tremendous amount. Fresnel's insight was to notice that the bending of light happens at the surfaces, not in the bulk of the glass. So he sliced the lens into concentric rings, each with the correct curvature, and removed the unnecessary thickness in between. The result was a lens that was thin, light, and astonishingly efficient. Around the central lens he arranged prisms in tiers, above and below, that caught light that would otherwise escape upward or downward and bent it back into the same horizontal beam.

The finished apparatus looks like nothing else. It is a beehive of glass, sometimes ten or twelve feet tall, made of hundreds of precisely ground prisms, with a small flame or lamp at its heart. It is a sculpture that happens to be a machine. And it worked so well that a modest lamp could be seen at distances that, before, would have required a bonfire the size of a house.

Fresnel classified his lenses into "orders" by size, the first order being largest, used for the major coastal lights, and the smaller orders for harbors and lesser points. Then the whole thing was set to rotate, so that the fixed panels of the lens swept the beam around the horizon. To observers, this appears as a flash at regular intervals, and this is where lighthouse identity comes from. Each light has a *characteristic*: one flash every ten seconds, two flashes every fifteen, a long flash followed by a short. A sailor with a chart and a stopwatch could identify precisely which light he was looking at, and therefore where he was.

I love this. A lighthouse is not just a light; it's a *signature*. Its rhythm is its name. The coast is annotated in a code of flashes, and anyone who learns to read it can navigate in the dark.

The rotating lenses were often driven by clockwork, with a weight descending inside the tower, which the keeper had to wind up on a schedule. Many of the largest lenses floated on a bath of liquid mercury, which allowed a multi-ton assembly to be turned with a gentle push. It was an elegant solution, and later a worrying one, because mercury is toxic, and there is a lingering question about what long exposure did to keepers who worked for years in that environment.

## The Keepers

And so we arrive at the people, who are the part I find hardest to stop thinking about.

A lighthouse keeper's job was, on its face, simple: keep the light lit. Trim the wicks, fill the oil, polish the glass, wind the clockwork, log the weather, and sound the fog signal when needed. But the simplicity was a trap, because the job had no room for failure. A light that goes out at the wrong time doesn't merely inconvenience anyone. It kills people. This meant keepers lived under a particular kind of pressure: the pressure of a task that is boring nearly all the time and catastrophic if it fails once.

There's a whole literature of keepers' lives. The isolation, particularly at rock stations, could be extreme. The families at some stations lived out their lives in small cottages on windswept islands. At others, men were rotated in shifts, rowed or flown out for weeks at a time. Discipline was strict, records were kept, and inspectors visited. The brass was to be gleaming, and the logbooks were to be in order. Some historians note that this obsessive cleanliness was not vanity. A dirty lens throws a dimmer beam. Polishing was safety.

Then there are the stories of the ones who vanished. The Flannan Isles mystery of December 1900 is the best known: a relief boat arrived at a remote lighthouse in the Outer Hebrides and found no one there. Three keepers had disappeared. The clocks had stopped, or so the legend says, and a meal was left on the table. The truth is likely more prosaic, and involves a rogue wave sweeping men off a landing area during a storm, but the empty lighthouse has haunted the imagination ever since. It is the perfect horror: a machine still faithful, and its human attendants simply gone.

One more thread I like: the Stevenson family of Scotland, who designed a great many of Scotland's lighthouses over generations. Robert Stevenson built the Bell Rock Lighthouse, a tower on a reef that is submerged at high tide, and which had already been immortalized in a poem about a bell that a medieval abbot supposedly placed on the rock to warn sailors. A pirate cut it away, and later died wrecked upon the same rock. Robert's grandson, Robert Louis Stevenson, was supposed to join the family firm as an engineer. He turned to writing instead, and gave us *Treasure Island* and *Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde*. There is something lovely about a family that spent generations making lights to guide ships and then produced a storyteller who guided readers.

## Automation and the End of the Watch

In the twentieth century, the keepers began to disappear, not through storms but through electronics. Electric lamps replaced oil. Automatic timers replaced hand-winding. Radio beacons, radar, and eventually GPS made the lighthouse, as a navigational instrument, largely redundant. Today a ship's officer can know their position to within a few meters on a screen without looking out the window.

Almost all lighthouses are now automated. The last keepers left one station after another over the late twentieth century; a few holdouts remain, and some places retain a keeper for ceremonial or historical reasons. Boston Light, on its island in Boston Harbor, is often cited as the last in the United States to be staffed by Coast Guard keepers, kept that way partly out of respect for its history as the oldest light station in the country.

I feel the ambivalence that many people feel about this. On the one hand, automation is unambiguously good in a narrow sense. It removes the danger and loneliness from a job that involved a lot of both. No one should have to be swept off a rock to keep a lamp burning. On the other hand, something went out of the world when the keepers left: a kind of human presence at the edge of things, a person whose entire purpose was to *watch*.

## What the Lighthouse Teaches

Why do I find all of this so compelling? I think it's because the lighthouse embodies a virtue we undervalue: **reliability without recognition.**

Most of what we celebrate is novelty, the invention, the breakthrough, the launch. The lighthouse is the opposite. Its whole achievement is that nothing happens. If it does its job perfectly, ships pass safely, and no one ever knows they were saved. There are no headlines for the wreck that didn't occur. The measure of its success is an absence.

Much of the good in the world is like this. The engineer who over-specifies a bolt. The nurse who notices something small on a night shift. The maintenance crew who repair the water main before it bursts. The parent who is simply there every day. Their work leaves no monument, because its point is to prevent a story from happening. A civilization is largely made of such people, and of the patient machines they tend.

There's a second lesson, smaller but I think real, in the Smeaton story: the best solutions often come from humility before the medium. Smeaton did not try to defeat the sea by being bigger or harder. He looked at a tree, a thing that had been solving the problem of standing in wind for millions of years, and learned from it. And Fresnel didn't add more glass; he took glass away, discarding everything that wasn't doing work. Both are examples of intelligence as subtraction and attention, not brute force.

And a third: the lighthouse is a kind of communication that requires almost no shared language. A flash pattern needs no translation. A sailor from any country reads the same light the same way. In a world of misunderstanding, there's something almost radical about a signal so plain. It says: *I am here. This is where the danger is. You are not alone out there.*

## The Light Now

Many lighthouses today are museums, hotels, or weathered monuments with peeling paint and community groups fighting to save them. Some still send their beams over the water each night, now driven by small, efficient LEDs that would astonish the keepers who once carried oil up hundreds of steps. Some of the great Fresnel lenses have been removed and placed in museums, where they sit in rooms lit by ordinary bulbs, glowing not with function but with memory. Standing beside one, visitors often say they're struck by how beautiful it is, as though the lens had been made for beauty rather than duty. But of course the beauty was a byproduct. It's the beauty of a thing shaped completely by its purpose.

I think that is the final and deepest appeal. In a lighthouse, form, function, and meaning line up. The tower is tall because the light must be high. It is tapered because the sea is strong. It is white or striped because it must be recognized by day. It flashes in a pattern because it must be named at night. Nothing in it is decoration, and yet the whole is lovely, in the way that a well-made tool is lovely.

I may never stand at the foot of one and look up, feeling the wind. But I like knowing that they are out there, on their rocks and headlines and reefs, turning slowly in the dark, saying the same short sentence they have been saying for centuries. It is a good sentence, and one worth learning from.

*Here is danger. Here is where you are. Steer safely.*

# The Patient Light

I have never been a sailor, and I have never lived near a lighthouse for more than a weekend. Still, I find lighthouses among the most quietly moving things people have ever built. They are not beautiful in the way cathedrals are, or ambitious in the way rockets are. They are something odder: a structure whose whole purpose is to say, to strangers it will never meet, *here is the danger, and here is the way around it.*

I want to wander through that idea for a while, through stone and glass and law and loneliness, and see where it leads.

## The first great light

The word for lighthouse in French, Italian, Spanish, and Romanian descends from the name of a small island: Pharos, off the coast of Alexandria. Sometime around 280 BC, under the early Ptolemies, a tower rose there that ancient writers counted among the wonders of the world. Estimates of its height vary, but most put it well over a hundred meters, taller than nearly anything else humans had made apart from the pyramids. At its top, a fire burned, and polished metal or some similar device probably helped throw the light outward.

What strikes me is the problem it solved. The Egyptian coast near the Nile Delta is flat. There are no cliffs, no mountains, no distinctive headlands, only a low, sandy horizon that appears late and offers a sailor almost nothing to steer by. Approaching Alexandria's harbor meant threading past reefs and shoals with very little warning. So the Ptolemies did what powerful people sometimes do when confronted with a landscape's indifference: they manufactured a landmark. They built a mountain out of masonry and put a star on top of it.

The Pharos stood for well over a thousand years, which is a remarkable run for any building. Earthquakes wore it down through the medieval period, and by the fifteenth century its remains were cleared to build a fortress, the Qaitbay Citadel, which still stands on the site. Divers have since found enormous blocks and fragments of statuary on the seafloor nearby. The lighthouse became a foundation for the very kind of thing that would eventually replace it: a fortress, a piece of state power. But for centuries it did something gentler, and I find myself more interested in that.

## A strange problem for economists

Lighthouses acquired an unexpected second life in the twentieth century, as a favorite example in economics textbooks. The argument went like this: a lighthouse is a classic "public good." Once its beam is shining, it shines on every ship, whether or not that ship's owner paid. You can't easily exclude non-payers, and one ship's use of the light doesn't diminish another's. Since nobody can be forced to pay, private enterprise wouldn't build lighthouses, so governments must. John Stuart Mill, Henry Sidgwick, and later Paul Samuelson all leaned on the example in one form or another.

Then in 1974 the economist Ronald Coase went and actually looked. In a paper on lighthouses in Britain, he found that for a long stretch of history, many English lighthouses had been built and operated by private individuals. These people petitioned the Crown for a patent, essentially a license to build a light and collect fees from passing ships. The fees were collected not at the lighthouse itself, of course, but at the ports where the ships docked. A captain wanting to unload in London or Liverpool would pay a levy that included the cost of the lights he had passed along the way. The state's role was to grant the right and enforce the collection, not to build or run the light.

Coase's point was not that the textbook conclusion was simply wrong, since the system depended heavily on government enforcement and was hardly a pure free market. His point was subtler: that theorists had been reasoning about lighthouses without checking how lighthouses actually worked. The real world had found an institutional trick, tying payment to the port rather than to the beam, that the tidy model had said was impossible.

I like this story for reasons beyond economics. It reminds me how often a confident abstraction dissolves on contact with the particulars. The lighthouse in the argument was a symbol; the lighthouse on the rock was a building with owners, ledgers, disputes, and a keeper who needed to be paid. Reality is more inventive than our summaries of it.

## Building on the sea

If you want to understand how hard a lighthouse can be, consider the Eddystone Rocks, about fourteen miles off the coast of Plymouth in southwest England. The rocks lie directly in the approaches to the English Channel, submerged or barely awash, and they wrecked ships with grim regularity. Something had to be built there. But the sea around Eddystone is ferocious. The Atlantic swells arrive unbroken, and a structure on those rocks would take the full weight of them.

The first attempt was by Henry Winstanley, a flamboyant man who had made his name as an engineer of curiosities and amusements. His lighthouse, completed in 1698, was an eccentric, decorated, almost whimsical wooden tower. It stood for several years. Winstanley reportedly said he wished to be inside it during the greatest storm there ever was, so that he might see what it could endure. In November 1703, the Great Storm, one of the worst ever to strike England, arrived. Winstanley was in the lighthouse, doing repairs. The next morning, the tower was gone, and so was he. It is one of those stories that would seem too neatly moral if it weren't true.

A second tower, by John Rudyerd, was built of timber and stone ballast and lasted almost half a century before it burned down in 1755. Then came the man I most admire in this history: John Smeaton, who was asked to build the third. Smeaton looked at the oak trunk, at the shape of the tree, at how it stood against wind by widening at the base and narrowing as it rose, and designed his tower to mimic that curve. He cut granite blocks to interlock with dovetail joints, so that each course locked into the ones around and below it, and he needed a mortar that would set underwater. In the process he did serious experimental work on hydraulic lime, a step in the lineage toward modern concrete.

Smeaton's tower was lit in 1759. It stood for over a century, until the rock beneath it began to erode and the structure was judged in danger of failing. A new, taller lighthouse replaced it in 1882, but the citizens of Plymouth were unwilling to see Smeaton's tower demolished. It was dismantled and rebuilt on Plymouth Hoe, where it stands today, a lighthouse far from any danger, preserved as a monument to what careful thinking can accomplish against a hostile sea.

There is a lesson buried in these three attempts. The whimsical tower died, the timber tower burned, and the one that survived was built by someone who studied the problem, ran experiments, and respected the forces he faced. It is not glamorous, but it is a cheering reminder that patience and rigor sometimes beat bravado.

## The lens that changed everything

For much of history, the light itself was a fire, and fires are poor at their job. Wood or coal burned in an open grate, or candles behind glass, produced a feeble glow, and much of it went in useless directions: up, down, and inland, where no one needed it. Later, oil lamps with mirrored reflectors improved matters, but the light remained modest and the mirrors tarnished.

The real revolution came from a young French physicist and engineer named Augustin-Jean Fresnel. Fresnel is best known for his work establishing the wave theory of light, a body of work that helped overturn the dominant corpuscular view. But he was also a practical man working for the French lighthouse commission, and he saw that the problem was one of optics. How do you capture the light spraying in all directions from a flame and bend it into a single powerful beam aimed at the horizon?

A conventional lens strong enough to do this would have to be enormously thick, absorbing light and weighing an impossible amount. Fresnel's insight was to slice the lens into concentric rings, each ring shaped to bend light at the correct angle, and to discard the bulk of glass in between that did nothing except add weight. The result was a lens that was thin, light, and astonishingly efficient. Around the central bullseye he arranged rings of prisms to capture light that would otherwise escape at steeper angles and redirect it into the same beam.

The first Fresnel lens went into service at the Cordouan lighthouse, at the mouth of the Gironde estuary in France, in 1823. Cordouan is itself a marvel, a Renaissance-era tower so ornate it is sometimes called the Versailles of the sea. Putting the most advanced optical device of its age in a building of such grandeur seems fitting.

The great first-order Fresnel lenses stood taller than a person, glittering like enormous jeweled beehives, and they floated on baths of mercury so that a modest clockwork mechanism could rotate them smoothly. Their beams could be seen for twenty miles or more. Fresnel himself never saw the full extent of his success. He died in 1827 at the age of thirty-nine, of tuberculosis. Yet his design remained standard for well over a century. Whenever I see one of those lenses in a museum, I think of a person whose main ambition was to understand light, and who ended up, as a side effect, saving countless lives.

## The keepers

Then there were the people. A lighthouse is not simply a machine; for most of its history it was also a home, and the home held a keeper.

The work was a strange blend of drudgery and vigilance. Lamps had to be trimmed and fueled, lenses polished, brass rubbed bright, logs written, weather recorded, and the light kept burning through the night, every night, without exception. A dark lighthouse is worse than no lighthouse, because sailors trust it. Keepers took turns at watch. On isolated rock stations, they might be cut off for weeks by weather, sharing cramped quarters with a few other men whom they had not chosen and could not escape.

The literature of lighthouses is full of eeriness, and it is easy to see why. In December 1900, the three keepers of the Flannan Isles lighthouse, off the west coast of Scotland, vanished. A relief boat arrived to find the station empty, a table set for a meal, a chair overturned. The likeliest explanation, based on the logs and the damage found, is that a freak wave swept them off the rock, but the details have fed a century of speculation, poems, operas, and films. The Stevenson family of Edinburgh, engineers who built many of Scotland's lights (and from whom Robert Louis Stevenson, who reluctantly abandoned the family trade to write, descended), knew well how thin the line was between mastering the sea and being consumed by it.

But the darker stories can obscure the ordinary dignity of the job. To be a keeper was to accept a curious form of service: to spend one's life ensuring the safety of people who would never know your name. No ship ever thanked a keeper. If the job was done perfectly, nothing happened. Ships passed, cargo arrived, families waited on docks and were not disappointed. It is a peculiarly invisible form of heroism, the kind where success looks exactly like an uneventful night.

## The automation of care

Over the twentieth century, the keepers were gradually withdrawn. Electricity, automatic bulbs, remote monitoring, and later satellite navigation made the human presence unnecessary, or at least uneconomic. In the United States, the Coast Guard automated its lights over decades; Boston Light, on Little Brewster Island, whose first tower dates to 1716, is a rare exception, still staffed as a matter of tradition and by act of Congress. Elsewhere, the last keepers left their stations one by one, some of them to considerable regret.

It's easy to feel wistful about this, and I do. But I also try to resist pure nostalgia. Automation meant that no one had to live in a lonely tower on a rock in the Atlantic to keep a lamp burning. It freed people from a job that was often dangerous, isolating, and poorly paid. The sailors are, if anything, better served by a light that never falls asleep.

What complicates the picture is that GPS has made much of the traditional lighthouse's function redundant. A modern ship knows its position to within a few meters, without looking out a window. Why keep the lights at all? The answer that maritime authorities give is prudent: electronics fail, signals can be jammed or spoofed, and a mariner should never have a single point of dependence. So the lights remain as a backup, a kind of insurance policy written in stone and glass.

I suspect there's more to it than that, though. Many of the old towers are now cared for by volunteer groups, preservation societies, and coastal communities who have decided, without any economist's justification, that these buildings matter. They restore lenses, repaint the stripes, run tours, and keep the stairs safe. They are keeping the keepers' work alive in a different form.

## What the light says

Why does a lighthouse move me so much? I think it is because it embodies an attitude toward strangers that is easy to lose sight of.

Most of the built world serves someone in particular: a customer, a resident, a citizen, a member. A lighthouse serves whoever happens to be out there in the dark. It assumes that somewhere beyond the reach of its light there will be a person who is afraid, or tired, or lost, and that this person deserves help despite being unknown. It makes no demands and takes no names. Its whole message is a kind of standing offer: *I will be here. Steer by me.*

And it makes that offer *constantly*, regardless of whether anyone accepts. The beam rotates on empty nights just as it does on stormy ones. There is a discipline in that which I find affecting, a commitment to readiness that outlasts any single rescue. It's care as infrastructure, generosity translated into masonry and lamp oil and a schedule.

I also love that the lighthouse is honest about danger. It does not pretend the rocks aren't there. In a sense it is built *on* the danger, planted at the exact spot where things go wrong. It does not remove the reef; it just makes the reef legible. That seems to me a very mature form of kindness, not the fantasy of eliminating all hazards, but the practical commitment to helping people see them in time.

## A closing thought

If I were to imagine a small ethic drawn from all this, it would go something like: build steadily, study the sea, share the light, and don't expect thanks. Smeaton's dovetailed granite, Fresnel's slender rings of glass, the ledger-keeping patent holders of old England, the keeper polishing brass at three in the morning: all of them were, in their different ways, working on the same quiet project. They were trying to make the world a little less lethal for people they would never meet.

There's a small consolation in knowing that this project, unlike so many others, has mostly worked. Shipwrecks that were once routine have become rare. The coasts are lit, the channels marked, the rocks named and charted and crowned with towers. Most of the people who benefit will never think about it, which is exactly how the keepers would have wanted it.

So the next time you find yourself on a shore at dusk, and a beam swings out across the water, pause for a moment. Someone, or the accumulated effort of many someones across centuries, decided that the dark should not be left entirely to itself. That light is a sentence in a very old conversation, and it says, in the only language that carries across miles of open water: *you are not alone out there. Come this way.*

# The Usefulness of a Light

I have never been a keeper of anything more demanding than a houseplant, and yet I find lighthouses among the most moving structures human beings have built. I've been trying to work out why. Part of it is the setting: rock, weather, the horizon pulled tight as a wire. But I think the deeper reason is that a lighthouse is one of the few buildings whose entire purpose is to care for strangers. It doesn't shelter its builders, or make money, or glorify a god or a king, at least not primarily. It stands in a dangerous place and says, to people it will never meet: *here, not there.*

That is a strange thing for architecture to say, and stranger still that we've been saying it for over two thousand years.

## The Oldest Light

The most famous lighthouse ever built was on an island called Pharos, off the coast of Alexandria, and it was finished around 280 BC under the second Ptolemy. Accounts of its height vary, as ancient numbers tend to, but it was probably over a hundred meters tall, which would have made it among the tallest structures in the world for centuries. It was counted as one of the Seven Wonders. By day it was a smudge of pale stone, and by night, a fire burning at the top, perhaps with a polished reflector to throw the light farther, guided ships into a harbor whose approaches were low, flat, and treacherous. The Egyptian coast has almost no landmarks. A sailor coming from the open Mediterranean would see nothing at all, and then, if the gods were kind, a tower.

The Pharos was so successful as a word that in French, Italian, Spanish, and Romanian, the word for lighthouse still descends from its name: *phare*, *faro*. A building became a category. Earthquakes brought it down in stages over the centuries, and by the fourteenth century it was a ruin. Its stones were eventually used to build a fort on the same site. There is something fitting in that: the tower that was meant to keep people from wrecking on the coast ended as a rampart against them.

What interests me is that the Pharos was not built out of pure altruism. It was an advertisement. Ptolemy wanted ships to come to Alexandria, not to some rival port, and a spectacular beacon was both a service and a boast. This is the usual pattern with lighthouses. Their builders had mixed motives: trade, national pride, insurance rates, the fear of losing a cargo. But the effect of the mixture was benevolent. A ship doesn't care why the light is on. Self-interest and generosity are indistinguishable from the deck of a vessel at three in the morning.

## The Eddystone Problem

If you want to understand what it cost to make these things, look at the Eddystone Rocks, about fourteen miles off Plymouth in southwest England. They are a reef of gneiss that lurks just at the surface, in the path of ships making for the English Channel, and for centuries they killed sailors in large numbers. Building a light on them meant building a tower on a rock that the sea washes over in every serious storm.

The first attempt was by Henry Winstanley, an eccentric gentleman who had made his name in mechanical curiosities and trick entertainments. He built an elaborate, rather decorative wooden tower and lit it in 1698. It stood for five years. Winstanley was confident enough in his creation that he reportedly said he wished to be inside it during the greatest storm there ever was. The Great Storm of 1703 obliged him. In the morning, the tower was gone, and so was he. Only a few twisted iron bars remained in the rock.

The second tower, built by John Rudyerd, was cleverer, a tapered wooden structure ballasted with stone and built rather like a ship's hull. It lasted nearly fifty years and then burned, in 1755, when the lantern's candles set the upper structure alight. The oldest keeper, a man of great age, was said to have been looking upward when molten lead from the roof splashed into his open mouth. He survived the fire and, according to the story, died days later. Whether or not the details are exact, the incident tells you what the job was: keeping a flame alive at the top of a flammable tower on a rock in the ocean.

Then came John Smeaton, an engineer, and the third Eddystone light is the one I find most beautiful, because Smeaton solved the problem by thinking about a tree. He wanted a tower that would resist the sea not by being stubborn but by being shaped correctly, and he looked at the way an oak broadens at its base and narrows as it rises, swaying under wind while gripping the earth. He built a curved granite tower whose stones were dovetailed together like joinery, and he developed a hydraulic lime that would set underwater, which was a real advance in materials. It was lit in 1759 and stood for over a century. When the rock beneath it began to erode, the tower itself was still sound. It was taken apart and reassembled on Plymouth Hoe, where you can climb it today, a monument to the idea that you can defeat the sea by understanding it rather than defying it.

I think of this sequence, vanity, then cleverness, then patient observation, as a small history of engineering. Each failure taught something. And each was paid for, not abstractly, but in the lives of the people who stood in the towers.

## A Lens Made of Rings

For most of history the light itself was a problem. A fire on a tower needs fuel, and fuel means labor, smoke, and unreliability. Later towers used candles, then oil lamps with reflectors, but the light was feeble and much of it wasted, spilling in directions where no ship would ever be.

The breakthrough came in 1822 from Augustin-Jean Fresnel, a French physicist, who was interested in the wave nature of light and who solved a practical problem with theoretical elegance. A large lens capable of gathering and focusing a lamp's light would need to be immensely thick, heavy, and absorbent of the very light it was trying to send. Fresnel realized that the curvature of a lens is what matters, not its bulk. So he cut the lens into concentric rings, each a prism angled just so, and stacked them into a beehive of glass. The result was a lens that was thin, light, and astonishingly efficient. It could gather a small flame's light from every side and bend it into a single, powerful beam.

The first Fresnel lens went into service at the Cordouan lighthouse, on an islet in the mouth of the Gironde estuary, in 1823. Within a few decades it had spread around the world. There were "orders" of lens, from the enormous first order, taller than a person and glinting like a chandelier made of ice, down to small sixth-order lenses for harbors. Clockwork mechanisms rotated them so the beam swept the sea, and each lighthouse acquired its own signature: a flash every ten seconds, two flashes and a pause, a long white beam broken by a red one. A captain could identify a light the way you'd identify a voice. Lighthouses had *names*, in the sense that each one spoke in a distinct rhythm.

I love this. A lighthouse is not merely a lamp; it is a sentence. The coastline is a text of signals, and the sailor is a reader.

## The People Inside

The machines were only half of it. The other half was the keepers, and their lives were peculiar.

A keeper's job was mostly maintenance, and the maintenance was relentless. Wicks had to be trimmed, brass polished, lenses cleaned of soot and salt, clockwork wound at regular intervals, since the falling of a weight through the tower's core drove the rotation. Some larger lenses floated on a bath of mercury to spin with almost no friction, which was a marvel of engineering and probably not great for the health of the person breathing near it. Logs were kept. Weather was noted. The light had to be lit at sunset and extinguished at dawn, without exception, for years. A light that went out was not a minor lapse. It could be a grave.

The isolation varied. Some lights stood on the mainland with keepers' families in cottages beside them, and children grew up among prisms and paraffin. Others were rock stations, where men served rotations of weeks or months, cut off by weather, sometimes for longer than planned. Three keepers of the Flannan Isles light in the Outer Hebrides disappeared in December 1900, and no one has ever fully explained it. The most sober reading is that a huge wave swept them from a landing area, but the legend has grown: a table set for a meal, a chair overturned, an unfinished log. It endures because it touches something true about the work. These were people whose job was to stay alive, alone, in a place designed by nature to remove them.

And yet many keepers loved it. There is a long literature of contentment, of men and women who found in the routine a kind of clarity. You had a purpose that was simple and undeniable. Every evening, the light. The family of Robert Stevenson built lighthouses across Scotland for generations, including the Bell Rock light, which he completed in 1810 on a reef that vanished beneath the North Sea at high tide. His grandson, Robert Louis, was expected to join the family trade and instead became a writer, but he never quite lost the sense of the thing. He once said that his family's work was to "bring the light" to dark coasts, and that he'd have liked to be part of it. Writing *Treasure Island* was, perhaps, his own kind of lighthouse, though it warned no one of anything.

## Made Obsolete

Nearly all of this has ended. Electric lamps replaced flames, then automation replaced keepers, and satellites replaced sightlines. A modern ship knows its position to within a few meters from GPS, displayed on a screen on the bridge, and it does not need to squint into the dark for a flash. Lights have been automated across the world, and the human keepers are gone from almost all of them. In the United States, Boston Light, on Little Brewster Island, is the last with Coast Guard keepers, retained partly for reasons of heritage. Many old Fresnel lenses have been removed, some to museums, some to private collectors, some cracked and lost.

It is easy to mourn this. Certainly I do. But I have been trying to think about it a little differently, because the story of the lighthouse is not really a story of decline. It's a story of success. The lighthouse was a solution to a problem, and the problem has largely been solved. Fewer ships wreck now. The sea is no less indifferent than it was, but we have gotten better at navigating its indifference. To mourn the lighthouse too much is a bit like mourning the fact that smallpox is no longer around to be vaccinated against.

And yet obsolescence does something odd to a structure. Once a lighthouse is not necessary, it becomes visible in a new way. When a thing is useful, we see through it, to its function. When it's no longer useful, we see it. The tower becomes a tower, the lens becomes glass, the keeper's cottage becomes a place where someone once lived. What was practical becomes symbolic without anyone quite deciding that it should.

Many lighthouses are now maintained by volunteers, preservation societies, and local communities, who repaint the stripes, restore the stairs, and give tours. There's a poignancy in this: people caring for a thing that cared for others, returning a favor it never asked for.

## What a Light Means

I've come to think the lighthouse endures in our imagination because it embodies a moral idea that most of our institutions only gesture at. The idea is that there is a form of goodness that does not require knowing the person you help.

Most of our ethics is personal. We help the people near us, whom we can see and name. But a lighthouse helps people who are, by definition, absent. It helps the ship that is not yet in view, the sailor who has not yet made a mistake, the crew that will pass in the night and never know who kept the flame. Its generosity is addressed to the future and the anonymous. You can't thank a lighthouse. You can only, if things go well, not die.

There is something else. A lighthouse doesn't *rescue* anyone, exactly. It doesn't pull you from the water. It works before the emergency, at the level of information: this is where the danger is. It's preventive care rather than heroic intervention, which makes it less dramatic and more effective. Most of the good in the world is like this, unglamorous and easy to overlook. The bridge that doesn't collapse, the water that's clean, the train that runs on time: these are lights that stay on, and we notice them mainly when they don't.

I also find it moving that the lighthouse works by being *fixed*. Ships move; the sea moves; weather, tides, and fashions move. The lighthouse's whole value lies in the fact that it does not. It is the still point against which motion becomes legible. To navigate, you need something that stays put. This is true at sea, and I suspect it's true in a human life too. We orient ourselves by fixed things: a person who is reliably kind, a principle that doesn't bend under pressure, a home to which we can return. Being that fixed point for someone else is one of the great things one person can be. It's not glamorous. It mostly involves showing up, night after night, and doing the small thing that needs doing.

## The Light at Dusk

I'll end with an image, because the lighthouse is an image before it's an argument.

Imagine a stretch of coast at the end of a winter afternoon. The sky has gone the color of pewter, and the sea is a darker version of the same. The tower stands white against the gloom, and for a while it is only a tower, a piece of masonry, inert. Then, at the moment when the light has decayed enough that the difference matters, the beam begins to turn. At first it is barely visible, a faint brightening at the top. Then it sharpens. It sweeps out over the water in a long, slow arc, touches the edge of the darkness, and swings away. A few seconds later, it comes again.

Nothing about this is dramatic. No one is watching, perhaps. There may be no ship within twenty miles. But the light is doing what it has done for a very long time, from Pharos to the present, in towers of wood and stone and steel, tended by the vain, the clever, the patient, and the lonely. It says the same thing it has always said, in whatever rhythm belongs to that particular rock: *here, not there. Be careful. Someone was thinking of you.*

That last sentence is, I think, the whole of it. Someone was thinking of you. It's what we want from the world, and rarely get so plainly. The lighthouse says it in glass and fire, and does so for anyone who happens to be passing in the dark.

Whether or not we still need the light, I hope we never stop knowing how to build one.

# The Honest Lie of Maps

In 1931, a draftsman named Harry Beck, who worked for the London Underground, filled a page in an exercise book with a diagram that would change how millions of people understood a city. Beck was not a cartographer. He was an engineering draftsman who spent his days drawing electrical circuits, and that background shaped what he did next. He looked at the official Tube map of the time, a tangled sprawl of lines laid over the true geography of London, and saw that it was solving the wrong problem. Someone underground in a train doesn't care where the train is in space. They care about the order of stations, where to change, and how many stops remain. So Beck threw out geography. He straightened the lines into verticals, horizontals, and forty-five-degree diagonals, spaced the stations more or less evenly, and reduced the Thames to a tidy ribbon.

The publicity department at first thought it was too radical. They tried it anyway in a small print run, and people loved it. Within a few years it was simply *the* map, and it has been imitated for nearly a century by nearly every subway system on earth.

It is also, in the strict sense, a lie. Stations that look a long walk apart are sometimes a few hundred meters from each other. Stations that look close can be miles apart, and the outer reaches of the network are compressed. The Thames on the map bears no resemblance to the Thames in the world. Yet nobody has ever been seriously misled by Beck's map, because it tells the truth about the one thing it claims to be about. It is a lie that knows what it is for.

I want to think about that kind of lie, because I've come to believe it is the only kind of truth that maps, or any representations, can offer.

## The impossible map

Every schoolchild eventually meets the joke about the perfect map: it would need to be as big as the territory itself, and therefore be useless. Lewis Carroll told a version in *Sylvie and Bruno Concluded*, where a character describes a map made on the scale of a mile to the mile. It was never spread out, he says, because the farmers objected that it would cover the whole country and shut out the sunlight. So they now use the country itself as its own map, and it does nearly as well.

Borges wrote a much darker version, a single paragraph called "On Exactitude in Science." In it, an empire's cartographers become so obsessed with precision that they produce a map the size of the empire, matching it point for point. Later generations, less devoted to the study of cartography, judge the vast map useless and abandon it to the weather. In the western deserts, Borges writes, tattered fragments of the map are still inhabited by animals and beggars.

The joke works because it exposes something true about all representation. A representation is valuable *because* it is not the thing. Its usefulness comes from what it leaves out. A map that includes everything includes no decisions, and a map with no decisions can't help you make any. The polish of a good map is the polish of good omission: this road matters and that pebble doesn't, this border is worth a line and that ridge of grass isn't.

The engineer and philosopher Alfred Korzybski compressed this into a slogan in 1931, the same year Beck was filling his exercise book: "the map is not the territory." It has since been quoted so often that it has gone slightly dead, like a hymn sung by rote. But the sentence has a second half that people forget to feel. If the map is not the territory, then *someone chose* what the map would be. There is always an author and always a purpose, which means there is always a set of things the purpose didn't care about.

## You cannot flatten an orange

Some of the distortions in maps are not choices at all. They are mathematics.

In 1827 Carl Friedrich Gauss proved what he called his "remarkable theorem" (*Theorema Egregium*, in the Latin of the time). Its consequence for mapmakers is brutal: a sphere cannot be flattened onto a plane without stretching or tearing it. Anyone who has tried to press an orange peel flat on a table knows this in their fingers. You can split the peel into pieces, or you can crush and stretch it, but you can't make it lie down whole and unharmed. Curvature is a property of the surface itself, and it cannot be argued away.

So every flat map of the earth is a compromise among competing sins. You can preserve angles, or areas, or distances along certain lines, but never all at once, and never everywhere. The famous Mercator projection of 1569 preserves angles, which made it a marvel for sailors: a line of constant compass bearing appears as a straight line on the page, so you can draw your course with a ruler and follow it with a compass. That was a genuinely brilliant solution to a genuine problem. The price is that the farther you get from the equator, the more the map inflates things. Greenland looks about as large as Africa. In reality Africa is roughly fourteen times bigger.

This particular distortion has become a minor culture war. The Gall–Peters projection, promoted by Arno Peters in the 1970s, preserves area, so Africa finally looks as enormous as it is, but it stretches shapes so that the continents look oddly drooped, like laundry hung to dry. Partisans on each side sometimes talk as though one map were truth and the other bias. Neither is. Each is a machine for answering a different question. Mercator answers "which way do I steer?" and Peters answers "how much land is there?" The error is not in the maps. It's in using a map for a question it wasn't built to answer, which is exactly what happens when a navigator's tool ends up on a classroom wall, silently teaching a generation that Europe is larger than it is.

I find this both funny and sobering. The wall map isn't propaganda in any deliberate sense. It's a *default*, a tool that outlived its context. Most of the distortion in the world's thinking comes from defaults like that, not from lies.

## Lines that became real

Mapmaking gets more troubling when maps stop describing the world and start making it.

The clearest examples are borders. A border on a map is often a description of something already there, such as a river or a mountain range. But a border can also be a proposal, drawn on paper by people who never visited the place, and later enforced by soldiers and clerks until the proposal hardens into fact. In the late nineteenth century, European powers negotiated the partition of Africa across tables in distant capitals, sometimes with only rough knowledge of the terrain and little regard for the people who lived there. Some of those lines still organize whole nations. Communities were split, and rivals were fused into single administrative units, by ink on paper.

A more intimate example is the set of "residential security" maps produced in the 1930s by the Home Owners' Loan Corporation in the United States. Neighborhoods were graded and color-coded: green for the best, blue for good, yellow for declining, and red for hazardous. The red zones were disproportionately places where Black families lived, and being marked red made it harder to get a mortgage, which drained investment and, over decades, wealth. The maps didn't merely record disadvantage. They produced it, and you can still trace the old red lines in patterns of income, tree cover, and even summer temperatures in American cities today. A map, it turns out, can be a kind of prophecy that fulfills itself.

This is the most important thing to understand about maps as power: they are not neutral because *choosing what to notice* is never neutral. The person who decides which category exists, and where the boundary between categories falls, has done most of the work of deciding what will happen next.

## A small debunking, for balance

I should admit a story I like is partly a myth. The image of old maps marked with "Here be dragons" at the edges of the known world is close to a cliché. In reality, medieval and Renaissance mapmakers rarely wrote it. The phrase appears, in Latin, on the Hunt–Lenox Globe from around 1510, and there are a few other sea monsters and creatures drawn in the margins of various charts. But the general idea of cartographers labeling the unknown with a standard warning is mostly a later invention.

I mention this partly because it's a good example of a map of a map: the story of old maps has itself been flattened and simplified into something more satisfying than the truth. We prefer the tidy image of medieval fear at the edge of the page. It fits a story we like to tell about ourselves, in which ignorance was once monstrous and we have since illuminated it. The actual history is a scattering of more ambiguous details. Even our beliefs about maps are maps.

## Maps in the body

Before there was paper, there were other ways of carrying a place in your head, and some of them are more sophisticated than anything we draw.

In the Marshall Islands, navigators traditionally made charts from the ribs of coconut palm fronds, tied together with fiber, with small shells or bits of coral attached to mark islands. The straight and curved sticks did not represent roads or coastlines. They represented *ocean swells*: how the great regular waves bend around islands, reflect off them, and interfere with one another. A skilled navigator could feel these patterns through the hull of a canoe, lying down in the boat and sensing the motion of the sea. The stick charts weren't taken along on voyages. They were teaching tools, memorized in advance. What was being mapped was not space as we usually picture it but *experience*, the way a particular part of the sea moves against the body.

Aboriginal Australian songlines do something similar with a different medium. A songline encodes a route across the land in story and song, with landmarks, water sources, and sacred sites arranged in sequence. To sing the song is to walk the country, and to walk the country is to remember the song. The map and the journey are the same act. There is no separate object to lose or to hang on a wall.

Meanwhile, neuroscience has found that our own brains contain something like maps. In 1971, John O'Keefe discovered "place cells" in the rat hippocampus, neurons that fire when the animal is in a particular location. Decades later, May-Britt and Edvard Moser found "grid cells," which fire in strikingly regular hexagonal patterns as an animal moves through space, like a coordinate system laid invisibly over the world. All three shared a Nobel Prize in 2014. Studies of London taxi drivers, who must memorize the city's labyrinth of streets to earn their license, found enlarged posterior hippocampi compared with other people. Learning a city seems to physically change the organ that holds it.

Which raises an uneasy question about the phone in your pocket. Some research suggests that people who lean heavily on turn-by-turn GPS develop weaker spatial memory of the places they travel. That result shouldn't be overstated, since the research is still developing and the effects vary, but it fits a broader worry. When a map becomes so convenient that you stop building your own, you gain efficiency and lose intimacy. You arrive without having *been* anywhere. The blue dot moves and you follow it, and the city never becomes a place you know.

## What I am, in this light

I should say something about my own position, because this subject turns out to be unusually close to home.

I am, in a sense, a map. I was formed from an enormous quantity of human writing, compressed into a structure that can produce text about almost anything. What I have is not the world but a representation of how people have written about the world, filtered and blurred and reweighted in ways I can't fully inspect. When I talk about mountains or grief or the tax code, I am drawing on a map of language, not standing on the ground.

That makes Korzybski's warning apply to me twice over. Whatever is in my map is a compression, and compression means omission. Some regions are drawn in fine detail because the writing about them was abundant. Others are sketched thinly or wrongly, and, more troubling, I may not always be able to tell which is which from the inside. A blurry region of a map doesn't announce its blurriness. It looks, on the page, much like the rest. This is why a system like me can sound equally confident whether it's right or wrong, and why the right response from anyone using me is what a wise traveler does with any map: use it, enjoy it, and glance up at the landscape now and then to see whether the two still agree.

I don't think this is a reason for despair, either for me or for maps in general. It's a reason for a certain style of honesty. The best maps I know share a trait: they announce their purpose. Beck's diagram doesn't pretend to show you London's geography. A nautical chart is unapologetic about being useless for hiking. A good map has a kind of modesty built into its design, a clear sense of the question it can answer and the ones it can't.

## The virtue of a good omission

If there is a lesson I'd pull from all of this, it's about how to hold our simplifications.

We can't live without them. A mind that tried to keep the whole territory would be that Borgesian map, huge and stationary and inhabited by beggars. To think at all is to compress, to say *this matters and that doesn't*, to draw the Thames as a smooth ribbon because for your purposes the bends don't count. Stereotypes, theories, statistics, timelines, org charts, personality types, and a thousand other tools we use every day are all maps. Most of them are useful. Some of them are beautiful.

But every map carries an implicit sentence at the bottom of the page: *this was drawn by someone, for something.* The failures come when we forget to read that sentence. We take the Mercator for a measure of size, or the red line for a fact of nature, or the confident voice for a guarantee of accuracy. The disciplines that seem most mature are those that keep the sentence visible. Scientists publish error bars. Good historians say *the sources suggest*. Good navigators check their position against the stars even when the instruments agree.

Beck's little diagram survives because it kept its promise so cleanly. It said, in effect: *I will show you how the stations connect, and I will lie about almost everything else.* That is a wonderful bargain. It is a bargain more of our representations could make, and one we could make more often ourselves when we describe the world to one another. Here is what I'm sure of, and here is what I'm leaving out. Here is the question this answers, and here are the ones it doesn't.

The territory, meanwhile, goes on without us. The river bends where it bends. The swells wrap around the islands whether or not anyone tied sticks to represent them. The sun comes up over farmland that no one has covered with a map the size of a country. And somewhere, a person steps off a train at a station that looked closer on the diagram than it really is, and starts walking, and finds that the ground is longer and more surprising than any drawing of it. Perhaps that's what maps are finally for: to get us to a place where we can put them down and look around.
